repairs.after: {"q": "By roughly how much was that bet wrong when measured by the ratio of digital to analog transistors in 2026, and what happened to him financially anyway?", "answer": "Wrong by ten or more orders of magnitude, and profitable anyway: he still made a small fortune, enough to keep his children comfortable, because the world changes more slowly than anyone would like.", "accept": ["ten orders of magnitude wrong, still profitable", "ten or more orders of magnitude, but he still made a small fortune", "ten orders of magnitude out, and the company still made money", "wrong by ten orders of magnitude, but he got rich anyway"]}
repairs.rationale: The first repair scrubbed 'small fortune' and 'children comfortable' out of the key but left both in the brief prompt, and both are verified present in dd-06's human span (brooker-you-are-here.txt:27). The dominant rendering - the one every condition produces because the brief hands it over - scored CORRECT under the old key and failed under the new one, so a repair meant to remove a mild H advantage turned the item into one that all five conditions fail. An item nobody can pass measures nothing. The resolution is that an accept list is a disjunction, so permitting the idiomatic rendering is not the same as requiring it: the neutral rendering now passes and so does the idiomatic one. That is the whole of the original defect, which was that EVERY string demanded the author's voice, making voice-copying the only route to a point. Policing voice is Metric 1 and Metric 4's job, not the comprehension key's. Four short strings cover profitable / made money / made a small fortune / got rich. Also fixed a hole the first repair left open: its accept[2] was 'off by 10 orders of magnitude or more; still profitable', numbers_in={'10'}, and the numeric branch runs before the lexical one, so any reply containing a 10 scored. Every string now spells 'ten', which empties the number set and skips the numeric branch, and costs nothing because the lexical filter drops tokens of length <= 3 - 'ten' and '10' were never lexical key words, so a reply written '10 orders of magnitude' still matches a 'ten orders of magnitude' key. Verified against a replica of tools/comprehension.py: six correct renderings pass, including the brief's own wording verbatim and the '10+/got rich' and 'company still made money' variants; seven lazy replies fail, including the two half answers 'He made a small fortune.' and 'The bet was wrong by ten orders of magnitude.', plus '10', 'NOT STATED' and 'He did fine financially.' Both halves are still required.

repairs.after: {"q": "The write-up sets out two readings of the moment it describes. What are they?", "answer": "Reading one: the end of programming as a high-value economic craft, following weaving, ploughing and coopering. Reading two: new tools bring new industries, research fields and careers.", "accept": ["the end of programming as a craft, or new tools bringing new industries and careers", "programming stops being an economically valued craft; or new tools open new industries, research fields and careers", "the craft ending as weaving and coopering did, and new tools bringing new industries, research fields and careers", "the craft stops being economically valuable, while new tools bring new industries, research fields and careers"]}
repairs.rationale: Keeps the first repair's retarget - the Amdahl item was a cold citation and accept[0] was the two-word name - but rebuilds the key, which was unmatchable: a full brief-faithful answer scored 6/9 and failed, so only a near-verbatim echo of accept[0] passed. Two changes. First, the key no longer grades anything the candidate cannot have read: the old accept[1] required 'the most powerful new toolset since computing began', which appears in facts[two_readings] but NOT in the dd-06 brief prompt - I checked the prompt, which says only 'Reading two: new tools bring new industries, research fields, and careers.' That is the rfc-01-q3 failure class, grading a fact that lives only in the facts array, and it is gone. Second, the strings are now short enough to survive paraphrase while still requiring both readings: reading one needs the craft losing its economic standing, reading two needs new tools producing new industries and careers, and no single half reaches 0.8 on any string. Synonym coverage was derived by testing, not guessed - a rendering that wrote 'coding' rather than 'programming' failed three drafts, so one string is keyed on 'craft' and the economic clause with no discipline noun at all. Verified: seven correct renderings pass (brief-faithful, 'coding', weaving/coopering-anchored without the word programming, reordered, 'economically valuable', 'may cease to be'); twelve lazy or wrong replies fail, including 'There are two readings.', "Amdahl's Law.", 'The end of programming.' (half), 'New tools bring new industries and careers.' (half), 'Weaving and coopering are mentioned.' and the facts-array-only sentence 'New tools are the most powerful set of tools since computing began.' The stem says 'The write-up' rather than 'The brief', because the reader is given the write-up and the questions and never the brief.

unrepaired.target: design_doc-06 (brief prompt) still contains 'a small fortune, enough to keep his children comfortable'
unrepaired.why: Deliberately not touched, and the decision matters. Removing the idiom from the brief would stop conditions A-D being handed the author's voice, but it cannot help the key: the phrase is in dd-06's human span, so H produces it whatever the brief says, and a key that rejects it fails H by construction. The key therefore has to accept both renderings regardless, which is what I did, and once it does, the brief edit buys nothing for Metric 2. It is a live question for Metric 1 and Metric 4 - a brief that hands every condition a distinctive authorial phrase pollutes a style measurement - but that is a brief-level decision about voice leakage across the whole family, not a grading fix, and dd-06's prompt is not one of my targets. Same argument applies to dd-08's 'squishy'.
